title: Investor Financing Options | Genstone Construction
metaDescription: Investor financing through Genstone Financial: DSCR rental loans, fix and flip loans, lines of credit and new construction loans, matched to renovation draws.
lede: The loan and the renovation are two halves of the same deal. Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans, fix and flip loans, lines of credit and new construction loans for real estate investors, from a single acquisition to a growing rental portfolio. Here's how each fits a strategy, and how financing and the renovation scope work together once the project starts.

sections.h2: Why financing and renovation should be planned together
sections.body:
On most investor deals, the renovation determines what the property is worth and the loan determines when the money for that renovation shows up. If those two plans are written separately, problems show up in the middle of the job. The lender's draw schedule might assume the kitchen is finished before the contractor has planned to get there. The loan amount might have been sized on a rehab budget that doesn't match the final scope. An inspector may arrive to approve a draw and find the work documented differently from how the lender expects to see it.

Genstone Construction and Genstone Financial are both part of the Genstone Companies. When the scope comes from one and the loan from the other, the line items, the draw schedule and the documentation can be lined up from the start. You can still use your own lender for a Genstone renovation, and Genstone Financial can finance projects renovated by others. The advantage of using both is fewer translation problems between the people funding the work and the people doing it.

A fix and flip loan is short-term financing built for buying a property, renovating it and selling it. These loans are typically structured with an acquisition portion that funds at closing and a renovation portion that's held back and released in draws as work is completed and verified.

What lenders usually look at on a flip: the purchase price, the renovation budget, the projected after repair value, the investor's experience, and the exit plan. That makes the quality of your scope and your ARV estimate part of the loan application, not just part of the construction plan. A detailed scope with labor, materials and a draw schedule, like the one Genstone provides after a Pre-Offer Rehab Review, gives the lender something specific to underwrite.

Because the loan is short-term, carrying costs on a flip depend heavily on how long the renovation takes. A realistic schedule, agreed before closing, helps you size the loan and your reserves correctly.

A DSCR loan is named for the debt service coverage ratio, a comparison of a property's rental income with its debt payments. Instead of relying mainly on your personal income, the lender looks at whether the property's rent covers the loan payment along with expenses such as taxes and insurance. That makes DSCR loans a common fit for buy-and-hold investors and for the refinance step of a BRRRR project.

The renovation feeds directly into a DSCR loan in two ways. First, the property's appraised value after the work sets how much can be borrowed. Second, the rent the property can command, often estimated by the appraiser, determines whether the ratio works. A renovation built for rentals (durable flooring, solid kitchens and baths, mechanical systems with life left in them) supports both.

On a BRRRR deal, it's worth talking to Genstone Financial about the refinance before the rehab begins. Knowing what the lender will look for helps you decide where the renovation budget will do the most good.

A line of credit gives an investor access to capital that can be drawn as needed and repaid, rather than a single lump sum tied to one property. For investors who buy regularly, it can shorten the time between finding a deal and being ready to close, and it can cover costs that fall outside a property-specific loan.

Lines of credit are often used alongside, rather than instead of, project loans. An investor might use the line to move quickly on an acquisition, then place longer-term financing once the property is renovated and stabilized. They can also help with timing gaps, such as covering a renovation stage while a draw is processed.

The terms and qualification requirements for a line of credit differ from those for property-level loans. Genstone Financial can explain how its line of credit programs are structured and whether one fits the way you buy.

New construction loans finance building a property from the ground up, typically releasing funds in stages as construction milestones are reached: foundation, framing, rough-ins, and so on through completion. Investors use them for infill lots, teardown-and-rebuild projects and spec homes.

The principles are the same as with a rehab loan, only with more stages. The lender needs a defined budget, a schedule, and a way to verify that each stage is complete before releasing the next draw. Clear documentation at every milestone keeps the funding moving. Genstone Financial offers new construction loans for investors who want to add new product to their portfolio or build for sale.

sections.h2: How renovation draws work with a loan
sections.body:
Genstone Construction doesn't take upfront payment. Construction draws are tied to completed work, and final payment is due after the project is complete and you've approved it. That structure lines up naturally with how most investor rehab and construction loans fund, which is also against completed and verified work.

A typical sequence looks like this:

- The scope and estimate set out the work, the cost and a draw schedule with defined milestones.
- The lender reviews the scope and budget as part of the loan and sets its own draw schedule, ideally matching the contractor's milestones.
- As each stage is finished, Genstone documents the work with photos and records, and lien waivers are collected for work that has been paid.
- The lender's inspector or reviewer verifies the completed stage and releases the draw.
- The process repeats through completion, followed by final billing after your approval.

Where things go wrong is in mismatches: a lender milestone that combines stages the contractor treats separately, or documentation that doesn't match what the inspector expects. Planning both schedules together avoids most of that.

sections.h2: Getting the numbers right before you apply
sections.body:
Every loan above depends on two numbers you supply or support: what the renovation will cost and what the property will be worth afterward. If either is off, the loan may be sized wrong, the draw schedule may not cover the real work, or the refinance may come in short.

That's the reason to start with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review from Genstone Construction. It estimates repair costs, helps refine the ARV, and checks whether the numbers support your offer before your capital is committed. You can also run a first pass through the ARV calculator on this site. With a scope and estimate in hand, the financing conversation is about a specific property and a specific plan.

faqs.q: Do I have to use Genstone Financial to renovate with Genstone Construction?
faqs.a: No. Genstone Construction works with investors using their own lenders, and with cash buyers. Using both companies can make it easier to align the scope, draw schedule and documentation, but it isn't required.

faqs.q: Which loan fits a BRRRR project?
faqs.a: Many BRRRR investors buy and renovate with short-term financing such as a fix and flip loan, then refinance into a DSCR rental loan once the property is renovated and rented. Genstone Financial can walk you through how that sequence works for a specific property.

faqs.q: Will the renovation scope help with my loan application?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Lenders underwriting a rehab need a credible budget and a credible after repair value. A detailed scope with labor, materials and a draw schedule gives them something specific to review.
